note: Theories, theoretical lenses, and framework approaches offered in Module 2. Each theory lists its constructs; a construct links to the shared construct vocabulary (library/constructs.json) where one matches (shared_construct_match: exact, close, or related). Paths are the theory's expected relationships between its constructs. citation_status 'added' marks citations added by maintainers that a reviewer should confirm. 'disciplines' lists ANZSRC 2020 Fields of Research divisions and groups (the HuMeta discipline vocabulary, standard/humeta/vocabularies.json) where the framework is widely used, for browsing. status 'draft' marks frameworks whose description, constructs, relationships, and links to shared constructs still need review by experts in the field; every theory and lens is a draft until the governance committee reviews it.

frameworks.label: Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)
frameworks.description: Behavior follows from intention, which is shaped by attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control.
frameworks.citation: Ajzen, I. (1991). The theory of planned behavior. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 50(2), 179-211.

frameworks.label: Self-Determination Theory (SDT)
frameworks.description: Satisfying needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness supports intrinsic motivation.
frameworks.citation: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68-78.

frameworks.label: Expectancy-Value Theory
frameworks.description: Achievement-related choices and performance depend on expectancies for success and the subjective value of the task.
frameworks.citation: Wigfield, A., & Eccles, J. S. (2000). Expectancy-value theory of achievement motivation. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 25(1), 68-81.

frameworks.label: Science Identity Model
frameworks.description: Science identity is built from competence, performance, and recognition as a science person.
frameworks.citation: Carlone, H. B., & Johnson, A. (2007). Understanding the science experiences of successful women of color: Science identity as an analytic lens. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 44(8), 1187-1218.

frameworks.label: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)
frameworks.description: Perceived usefulness and ease of use shape the intention to use a technology and its actual use.
frameworks.citation: Davis, F. D. (1989). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and user acceptance of information technology. MIS Quarterly, 13(3), 319-340.

frameworks.label: Health Belief Model (HBM)
frameworks.description: Health behavior depends on perceived threat, benefits, barriers, self-efficacy, and cues to action.
frameworks.citation: Rosenstock, I. M. (1974). The health belief model and preventive health behavior. Health Education Monographs, 2(4), 354-386.

frameworks.label: Social Cognitive Theory (SCT)
frameworks.description: Personal, environmental, and behavioral factors influence each other; self-efficacy and outcome expectations guide behavior.
frameworks.citation: Bandura, A. (1986). Social foundations of thought and action: A social cognitive theory. Prentice-Hall.

frameworks.label: Self-Efficacy Theory
frameworks.description: Self-efficacy is shaped by mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and emotional states.
frameworks.citation: Bandura, A. (1977). Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change. Psychological Review, 84(2), 191-215.

frameworks.label: Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Change)
frameworks.description: People move through stages of readiness to change a behavior.
frameworks.citation: Grimley, D., Prochaska, J. O., Velicer, W. F., Blais, L. M., & DiClemente, C. C. (1994). The transtheoretical model of change. In T. M. Brinthaupt & R. P. Lipka (Eds.), Changing the self: Philosophies, techniques, and experiences (pp. 201-227). SUNY Press.

frameworks.label: Control Theory
frameworks.description: Behavior is regulated by comparing a perceived current state with a goal and adjusting to reduce the discrepancy.
frameworks.citation: Carver, C. S., & Scheier, M. F. (1982). Control theory: A useful conceptual framework for personality-social, clinical, and health psychology. Psychological Bulletin, 92(1), 111-135.

frameworks.label: COM-B Model
frameworks.description: Behavior results from capability, opportunity, and motivation.
frameworks.citation: Michie, S., van Stralen, M. M., & West, R. (2011). The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions. Implementation Science, 6, 42.

frameworks.label: Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF)
frameworks.description: Fourteen domains that influence behavior, used to study implementation problems.
frameworks.citation: Atkins, L., Francis, J., Islam, R., O'Connor, D., Patey, A., Ivers, N., et al. (2017). A guide to using the Theoretical Domains Framework of behaviour change to investigate implementation problems. Implementation Science, 12, 77.

constructs.label: Social and Professional Role and Identity

frameworks.label: Operant Conditioning
frameworks.description: Behavior changes with its consequences: reinforcement and punishment.
frameworks.citation: Skinner, B. F. (1953). Science and human behavior. Macmillan.

frameworks.label: Sociocultural Theory
frameworks.description: Learning and thinking develop through social interaction and cultural tools.
frameworks.citation: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Harvard University Press.

frameworks.label: Communities of Practice / Situated Learning
frameworks.description: Learning is participation in communities of practice, moving from peripheral to full participation.
frameworks.citation: Lave, J., & Wenger, E. (1991). Situated learning: Legitimate peripheral participation. Cambridge University Press.

frameworks.label: Critical Race Theory
frameworks.description: Examines how race and racism shape law, institutions, and everyday life, centering the experiences of people of color.
frameworks.citation: Delgado, R., & Stefancic, J. (2017). Critical race theory: An introduction (3rd ed.). New York University Press.

frameworks.label: Intersectionality
frameworks.description: Examines how overlapping social identities and systems of power shape experience.
frameworks.citation: Crenshaw, K. (1989). Demarginalizing the intersection of race and sex. University of Chicago Legal Forum, 1989(1), 139-167.

frameworks.label: Feminist Theory
frameworks.description: Examines gender, power, and knowledge; a family of perspectives rather than a single theory. Cite the specific work you draw on.
frameworks.citation: hooks, b. (1984). Feminist theory: From margin to center. South End Press.

frameworks.label: Postcolonial and Decolonial Theory
frameworks.description: Examines the legacies of colonialism in culture, knowledge, and institutions. Cite the specific work you draw on.
frameworks.citation: Said, E. W. (1978). Orientalism. Pantheon Books.

frameworks.label: Phenomenology
frameworks.description: Studies lived experience as people experience it.
frameworks.citation: van Manen, M. (1990). Researching lived experience: Human science for an action sensitive pedagogy. State University of New York Press.

frameworks.label: Critical Theory
frameworks.description: Examines power, ideology, and social structures with the aim of social change. Cite the specific work you draw on.
frameworks.citation: Horkheimer, M. (1972). Critical theory: Selected essays (M. J. O'Connell et al., Trans.). Herder and Herder.

frameworks.label: New Historicism and Cultural History
frameworks.description: Reads texts and artifacts in relation to the cultural and historical conditions of their making.
frameworks.citation: Greenblatt, S. (1980). Renaissance self-fashioning: From More to Shakespeare. University of Chicago Press.

frameworks.label: Semiotics and Visual Rhetoric
frameworks.description: Analyzes how signs, images, and media make meaning.
frameworks.citation: Barthes, R. (1977). Image, music, text (S. Heath, Trans.). Hill and Wang.

frameworks.label: Bourdieu's Theory of Practice (Capital, Habitus, Field)
frameworks.description: Social position and practice arise from the forms of capital people hold, their habitus, and the fields in which they act.
frameworks.citation: Bourdieu, P. (1986). The forms of capital. In J. G. Richardson (Ed.), Handbook of theory and research for the sociology of education (pp. 241-258). Greenwood.

constructs.label: Economic capital
constructs.definition: Money and assets that can be directly converted into other resources.

constructs.label: Cultural capital
constructs.definition: Knowledge, skills, credentials, and tastes valued in a field.

constructs.label: Social capital
constructs.definition: Resources available through durable networks of relationships.

constructs.label: Habitus
constructs.definition: Durable dispositions, learned through social position, that shape perception and action.

constructs.label: Field
constructs.definition: A structured social arena (such as education or art) with its own stakes and rules.

constructs.label: Practice and outcomes
constructs.definition: What people do and achieve within a field, such as educational attainment.

frameworks.label: Social Capital Theory
frameworks.description: Networks, trust, and shared norms are resources that make collective action and individual outcomes possible.
frameworks.citation: Coleman, J. S. (1988). Social capital in the creation of human capital. American Journal of Sociology, 94, S95-S120.

constructs.label: Social networks
constructs.definition: Ties among people, within and across groups.

constructs.label: Trust
constructs.definition: Confidence that others will act reliably and cooperatively.

constructs.label: Norms and obligations
constructs.definition: Shared expectations, including reciprocity, that guide behavior.

constructs.label: Closure of community ties
constructs.definition: How densely people's contacts know each other.

constructs.label: Collective and individual outcomes
constructs.definition: For example civic engagement, school completion, or well-being.

frameworks.label: Symbolic Interactionism
frameworks.description: People act toward things on the basis of the meanings those things have for them, meanings that arise in and are modified through social interaction.
frameworks.citation: Blumer, H. (1969). Symbolic interactionism: Perspective and method. Prentice-Hall.

frameworks.label: Institutional Theory (Institutional Isomorphism)
frameworks.description: Organizations in the same field become alike through coercive, mimetic, and normative pressures, often in pursuit of legitimacy rather than efficiency.
frameworks.citation: DiMaggio, P. J., & Powell, W. W. (1983). The iron cage revisited: Institutional isomorphism and collective rationality in organizational fields. American Sociological Review, 48(2), 147-160.

constructs.label: Coercive pressure
constructs.definition: Formal and informal pressure from organizations an organization depends on, such as regulators or funders.

constructs.label: Mimetic pressure
constructs.definition: Copying organizations seen as successful, especially under uncertainty.

constructs.label: Normative pressure
constructs.definition: Pressure from professions, training, and professional networks.

constructs.label: Isomorphism
constructs.definition: Similarity of structures and practices across organizations in a field.

constructs.label: Legitimacy
constructs.definition: Being seen as appropriate within the field.

frameworks.label: Social Identity Theory
frameworks.description: Part of the self-concept comes from group memberships; people seek positive distinctiveness for their groups, which shapes intergroup behavior.
frameworks.citation: Tajfel, H., & Turner, J. C. (1979). An integrative theory of intergroup conflict. In W. G. Austin & S. Worchel (Eds.), The social psychology of intergroup relations (pp. 33-47). Brooks/Cole.

constructs.label: Social categorization
constructs.definition: Sorting oneself and others into social groups.

constructs.label: Group identification
constructs.definition: How strongly one identifies with a group.

constructs.label: Social comparison
constructs.definition: Comparing one's group with other groups.

constructs.label: In-group favoritism
constructs.definition: Favoring one's own group over others.

constructs.label: Self-esteem
constructs.definition: Positive self-evaluation derived from group membership.

frameworks.label: Civic Voluntarism Model
frameworks.description: People take part in politics when they can (resources), want to (engagement), and are asked (recruitment).
frameworks.citation: Verba, S., Schlozman, K. L., & Brady, H. E. (1995). Voice and equality: Civic voluntarism in American politics. Harvard University Press.

constructs.label: Resources
constructs.definition: Time, money, and civic skills.

constructs.label: Political engagement
constructs.definition: Interest, efficacy, information, and partisanship.

constructs.label: Recruitment
constructs.definition: Being asked to take part, through networks and institutions.

constructs.label: Political participation
constructs.definition: Voting, contacting officials, campaigning, protest, and other activity.

frameworks.label: Rational Choice Theory
frameworks.description: Explains political and social outcomes as the result of individuals pursuing their goals given costs, benefits, information, and the choices of others.
frameworks.citation: Downs, A. (1957). An economic theory of democracy. Harper & Row.

frameworks.label: Framing Theory
frameworks.description: Communicators select and make salient some aspects of a perceived reality, promoting a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, or remedy.
frameworks.citation: Entman, R. M. (1993). Framing: Toward clarification of a fractured paradigm. Journal of Communication, 43(4), 51-58.

constructs.label: Frames in the text
constructs.definition: How a message defines a problem, its causes, its moral evaluation, and remedies.

constructs.label: Audience frames
constructs.definition: The interpretive schemas audience members bring.

constructs.label: Interpretation and attitudes
constructs.definition: How audiences understand and evaluate the issue.

frameworks.label: Agenda-Setting Theory
frameworks.description: The prominence the news media give to issues shapes which issues the public considers important.
frameworks.citation: McCombs, M. E., & Shaw, D. L. (1972). The agenda-setting function of mass media. Public Opinion Quarterly, 36(2), 176-187.

constructs.label: Media agenda (issue salience in media)
constructs.definition: How much attention and prominence media give an issue.

constructs.label: Need for orientation
constructs.definition: An audience member's need for guidance on an issue.

constructs.label: Public agenda (perceived issue importance)
constructs.definition: How important the public considers an issue.

frameworks.label: Uses and Gratifications
frameworks.description: Audiences actively choose media to satisfy needs; the gratifications they seek shape media use and its effects.
frameworks.citation: Katz, E., Blumler, J. G., & Gurevitch, M. (1973). Uses and gratifications research. Public Opinion Quarterly, 37(4), 509-523.

constructs.label: Social and psychological needs
constructs.definition: Needs such as information, identity, social connection, and diversion.

constructs.label: Gratifications sought
constructs.definition: What people expect to get from a medium.

constructs.label: Media use
constructs.definition: Choice and amount of media and content.

constructs.label: Gratifications obtained
constructs.definition: What people report actually getting.

frameworks.label: Diffusion of Innovations
frameworks.description: New ideas, practices, and technologies spread through social systems over time; perceived attributes of an innovation shape how quickly it is adopted.
frameworks.citation: Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of innovations (5th ed.). Free Press.

constructs.label: Relative advantage
constructs.definition: How much better the innovation seems than what it replaces.

constructs.label: Compatibility
constructs.definition: Fit with existing values, experience, and needs.

constructs.label: Complexity
constructs.definition: How difficult the innovation seems to understand and use.

constructs.label: Trialability
constructs.definition: How easily it can be tried on a limited basis.

constructs.label: Observability
constructs.definition: How visible its results are to others.

constructs.label: Adoption
constructs.definition: The decision to make full use of the innovation.

frameworks.label: Human Capital Theory
frameworks.description: Education and training are investments that raise productivity and, in turn, earnings.
frameworks.citation: Becker, G. S. (1964). Human capital: A theoretical and empirical analysis, with special reference to education. National Bureau of Economic Research; Columbia University Press.

constructs.label: Investment in education and training
constructs.definition: Years and kinds of schooling, training, and experience.

constructs.label: Skills and knowledge
constructs.definition: Productive capacities acquired through investment.

constructs.label: Productivity
constructs.definition: Output per unit of work.

constructs.label: Earnings
constructs.definition: Wages and income.

frameworks.label: Ecological Systems Theory
frameworks.description: Development happens within nested systems, from immediate settings such as family and school to the wider culture, and through their interactions over time.
frameworks.citation: Bronfenbrenner, U. (1979). The ecology of human development: Experiments by nature and design. Harvard University Press.

constructs.label: Microsystem
constructs.definition: Immediate settings such as family, classroom, and peers.

constructs.label: Mesosystem
constructs.definition: Links between immediate settings, such as home and school.

constructs.label: Exosystem
constructs.definition: Settings that affect the person indirectly, such as a parent's workplace.

constructs.label: Macrosystem
constructs.definition: Cultural values, laws, and economic conditions.

constructs.label: Chronosystem
constructs.definition: Change over time, in the person and the environment.

constructs.label: Development
constructs.definition: The outcomes of interest, such as learning or well-being.

frameworks.label: Constructivism
frameworks.description: Learners actively build knowledge by connecting new experience to what they already know, rather than receiving it ready-made.
frameworks.citation: Piaget, J. (1952). The origins of intelligence in children (M. Cook, Trans.). International Universities Press.

frameworks.label: Cognitive Load Theory
frameworks.description: Working memory is limited; instruction that reduces unnecessary (extraneous) load frees capacity for building schemas.
frameworks.citation: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

constructs.label: Intrinsic load
constructs.definition: Load from the inherent complexity of the material for this learner.

constructs.label: Extraneous load
constructs.definition: Load from how information is presented, not needed for learning.

constructs.label: Germane load
constructs.definition: Effort devoted to building schemas.

constructs.label: Instructional design
constructs.definition: For example worked examples, integrated formats, or goal-free problems.

constructs.label: Learning and transfer
constructs.definition: Schema acquisition and later problem-solving performance.

frameworks.label: Community of Inquiry
frameworks.description: Deep learning in online and blended courses emerges from the interplay of social, cognitive, and teaching presence.
frameworks.citation: Garrison, D. R., Anderson, T., & Archer, W. (1999). Critical inquiry in a text-based environment: Computer conferencing in higher education. The Internet and Higher Education, 2(2-3), 87-105.

constructs.label: Social presence
constructs.definition: Participants' ability to project themselves socially and emotionally.

constructs.label: Teaching presence
constructs.definition: Design, facilitation, and direct instruction.

constructs.label: Cognitive presence
constructs.definition: Constructing meaning through sustained reflection and discourse.

constructs.label: Educational experience
constructs.definition: The quality of learning in the community.

frameworks.label: Culturally Relevant Pedagogy
frameworks.description: Teaching that supports students' academic success, cultural competence, and critical consciousness.
frameworks.citation: Ladson-Billings, G. (1995). Toward a theory of culturally relevant pedagogy. American Educational Research Journal, 32(3), 465-491.

frameworks.label: Funds of Knowledge
frameworks.description: Households and communities hold historically accumulated knowledge and skills that teachers can learn about and build on.
frameworks.citation: Moll, L. C., Amanti, C., Neff, D., & Gonzalez, N. (1992). Funds of knowledge for teaching: Using a qualitative approach to connect homes and classrooms. Theory Into Practice, 31(2), 132-141.

frameworks.label: Hermeneutics
frameworks.description: Understanding as interpretation: meaning emerges in a dialogue between the interpreter's horizon and that of the text or work.
frameworks.citation: Gadamer, H.-G. (2004). Truth and method (2nd rev. ed., J. Weinsheimer & D. G. Marshall, Trans.). Continuum. (Original work published 1960)

frameworks.label: Foucauldian Discourse Analysis
frameworks.description: Examines how discourses, the rules governing what can be said and known, produce knowledge, subjects, and relations of power.
frameworks.citation: Foucault, M. (1972). The archaeology of knowledge (A. M. Sheridan Smith, Trans.). Pantheon.

frameworks.label: Narratology
frameworks.description: Analyzes how narratives work: order, duration, voice, and focalization, and how they shape meaning.
frameworks.citation: Genette, G. (1980). Narrative discourse: An essay in method (J. E. Lewin, Trans.). Cornell University Press.

frameworks.label: Reception Theory and Reader-Response
frameworks.description: Meaning is realized in the encounter between a work and its readers or audiences, whose expectations change over time.
frameworks.citation: Jauss, H. R. (1982). Toward an aesthetic of reception (T. Bahti, Trans.). University of Minnesota Press.

frameworks.label: Queer Theory
frameworks.description: Questions fixed categories of gender and sexuality and examines how they are produced and performed.
frameworks.citation: Butler, J. (1990). Gender trouble: Feminism and the subversion of identity. Routledge.

frameworks.label: Ecocriticism
frameworks.description: Studies the relationship between literature, culture, and the physical environment.
frameworks.citation: Glotfelty, C., & Fromm, H. (Eds.). (1996). The ecocriticism reader: Landmarks in literary ecology. University of Georgia Press.

frameworks.label: Marxist Criticism
frameworks.description: Reads cultural works in relation to the economic and class relations of the society that produced them.
frameworks.citation: Eagleton, T. (1976). Marxism and literary criticism. University of California Press.

frameworks.label: Material Culture Studies
frameworks.description: Studies objects as evidence of the beliefs, values, and practices of the people who made and used them.
frameworks.citation: Prown, J. D. (1982). Mind in matter: An introduction to material culture theory and method. Winterthur Portfolio, 17(1), 1-19.

frameworks.label: Arts-Based Research
frameworks.description: Uses artistic processes and forms (writing, image, performance, music) as ways of inquiring and of representing what is learned.
frameworks.citation: Barone, T., & Eisner, E. W. (2012). Arts based research. SAGE.

frameworks.label: My own conceptual framework
frameworks.description: A framework you developed or adapted for this study. Describe it and list its concepts below.

frameworks.label: Exploratory or inductive (no framework chosen in advance)
frameworks.description: Concepts emerge from the data, as in grounded theory or other inductive approaches. You can still list concepts or codes as they develop.
